overview.title: Why scaling alone won't carry LLMs, and the chapter 16 summary (part 1)
overview.section: 16.5 Where are LLMs heading next? / Summary
overview.main_topic: The practical and data limits on simply making LLMs bigger, the role of reinforcement learning as a source of fresh training signal, and the first half of the chapter summary (LLM ingredients, sampling strategies, scale)
overview.central_idea: Parameter counts have stopped growing monotonically because deployment cost matters and because high-quality human text is running out; reinforcement learning in self-contained environments is one way to keep generating training signal. The deeper problem is that LLMs learn far less efficiently than humans, yet they already enable fluent natural-language interfaces built on a simple recipe: Transformer + next-token prediction + lots of unlabeled text, plus a sampling strategy at generation time.
overview.importance: This page closes chapter 16's argument about where LLMs are going (begun on p.528) with an honest assessment of their limits, and then distills the whole chapter into a few bullets you should be able to explain from memory.
learning_objectives: Explain two reasons why recent LLM parameter counts have not grown as steadily as dataset sizes
Describe the 'running out of data' problem and why training on LLM-generated text is risky
Explain why reinforcement learning in a self-contained environment can supply new training data
State the three ingredients of an LLM as summarized by the book
Distinguish greedy search, random sampling and top-K sampling
prerequisites: Compute budget trade-off between model size and data size (p.528–529)
Reasoning models trained with a simple RL loop (p.526–528)

summary:
The page finishes section 16.5. Building on figure 16.8 (p.529), the authors observe that **tokens used for pretraining have climbed steadily, while parameter counts have varied a lot since GPT-3**. Two reasons: GPT-3 is now known to have been *undertrained* for its size (p.528), and, practically, a smaller model that runs on cheaper hardware is often worth a small loss in quality, because a great model that is too expensive to serve is of limited use.

A second brake on naive scaling is **data scarcity**: companies are struggling to find more high-quality, public, human-written text, and models increasingly train on text produced by other LLMs ("eating their own tail"), which raises new concerns. This is one reason **reinforcement learning** is attracting attention: a difficult, self-contained *environment* that keeps generating new problems lets a model keep training on its own outputs instead of on scraped web text (compare the reasoning-model loop on p.527–528).

The authors then step back: none of these fixes is a silver bullet. The core problem is that **LLMs are wildly inefficient learners** compared to humans — their abilities come from reading orders of magnitude more text than any person ever will — so research into learning from limited data will continue alongside scaling. Still, fluent natural-language interfaces alone will reshape computing, and the chapter has shown the basic recipe behind them.

The **Summary** begins: an LLM combines (1) the Transformer, (2) a language-modeling task (predict the next token from past tokens) and (3) a large amount of unlabeled text. An LLM learns a probability distribution over the next token; a **sampling strategy** turns this into long text — *greedy search* (always the most likely token), *random sampling* (sample the full categorical distribution) and *top-K sampling* (sample only among the K most likely tokens). LLMs use billions of parameters and trillions of words of training text. The summary continues on p.531.

paragraphs.excerpt: We can note that while the total number of tokens used for pretraining has climbed
paragraphs.what_it_says: Reading figure 16.8: pretraining token counts have risen steadily and massively, but model parameter counts have varied substantially since GPT-3. Partly this is because GPT-3 is now known to have been undertrained; partly it is practical: when deploying, it is often worth sacrificing some performance for a smaller model that fits on cheaper hardware, since an excellent model that is prohibitively expensive to run helps little.
paragraphs.what_it_means: There are two separate optimization problems. Training-compute optimality (p.528) says that for a fixed flops budget, GPT-3 should have been smaller and trained on more data. Deployment economics adds another pressure: inference cost is paid for every query for the lifetime of the model, so teams often deliberately train a model *smaller* than compute-optimal and feed it even more tokens, accepting extra training cost to get a cheaper model to serve.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why 'bigger every year' is not the actual trend line, and why many popular open models (such as the 1-billion-parameter Gemma used on p.509) are small: the best model for a product is the one that is good enough and affordable at scale.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: training compute scales roughly as $C \approx 6ND$ (N parameters, D tokens), while inference cost per token scales with N. Lowering N and raising D keeps training compute similar but makes every future query cheaper.

terminology.meaning: A model that saw too few training tokens for its parameter count; more data (with fewer parameters) would have given better results for the same compute.
Running a trained model to serve predictions (inference), where memory and per-query cost dominate.

connections: p.528: a fixed pretraining budget buys a fixed number of flops, spent on either more data or more parameters; GPT-3 was too big for its budget.
p.529: figure 16.8 shows parameter counts (top) and dataset sizes (bottom) for LLMs from 2018 to 2025.
p.514: memory constraints of a 1B-parameter model during fine-tuning illustrate why size matters in practice.

paragraphs.excerpt: There’s another reason we might not be able to just scale up these models
paragraphs.what_it_says: We are starting to run out of pretraining data: companies have trouble finding more high-quality, public, human-written text. Models are even 'eating their own tail' by training on a significant amount of LLM-generated content, which brings new concerns. This is one reason reinforcement learning is getting attention: a difficult, self-contained environment that generates new problems lets a model keep training on its own output, without scraping the web for more quality text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Scaling laws assume you can keep increasing D, the number of tokens. If the supply of good human text is finite, D stops growing. Synthetic text from other models is a poor substitute because it reproduces (and can amplify) the source model's errors and narrows the diversity of the data. An RL environment changes the source of signal: instead of imitating existing text, the model attempts problems whose outcomes can be checked (for example, math answers or code that runs tests), and correct attempts become new training data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It reframes the next phase of LLM progress: the bottleneck is shifting from compute to data, and from imitation of human text to learning from verifiable feedback — exactly the loop described for reasoning models on p.527–528.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The 'environment' is the RL term for whatever produces observations and rewards. For an LLM it can be a generator of problems plus an automatic checker that rewards correct solutions.

terminology.meaning: The authors' image for models trained on text produced by other LLMs, a feedback loop that can degrade quality (sometimes called model collapse in the research literature — not a term the book uses).
In reinforcement learning, the system the agent acts in; here, a self-contained source of new problems and feedback for an LLM.

connections: p.527–528: sampling many chain-of-thought answers, keeping verified correct ones and fine-tuning on them is a simple RL loop.
p.519: RLHF uses a reward model trained on human preferences as a different kind of feedback signal.

paragraphs.excerpt: None of the solutions we touched on will be a silver bullet for the issues
paragraphs.what_it_says: No single fix will solve LLMs' problems. Fundamentally, LLMs are wildly inefficient learners compared to humans: their capabilities come only from training on many orders of magnitude more text than a person reads in a lifetime. As scaling continues, so will research into models that learn quickly from limited data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Even if compute and data keep growing, the gap in sample efficiency remains. A human becomes fluent and capable with a tiny fraction of the language exposure an LLM gets, which suggests LLMs are missing something about how to learn — they compensate with sheer volume rather than generalization from few examples.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is a sober counterweight to hype, and a direct preview of chapter 19's argument that deep learning models struggle to adapt to novelty and mostly reuse patterns memorized during training.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Inference (not in the book, rough order-of-magnitude reasoning): a person might read on the order of hundreds of millions of words in a lifetime, while frontier LLMs train on trillions of tokens — a gap of roughly four orders of magnitude.

terminology.meaning: How much data a learner needs to reach a given level of skill (not the book's term, but what 'inefficient at learning' refers to).

connections: p.589: chapter 19 argues LLMs fetch memorized 'vector functions' rather than genuinely adapting to novel problems.
p.494: GPT-3 already showed hallucination and poor adaptation to unfamiliar problems.

paragraphs.excerpt: Still, LLMs represent the ability to build fluent natural language interfaces, and that
paragraphs.what_it_says: Despite their limits, LLMs make fluent natural-language interfaces possible, which alone will massively change what we can do with computers. The chapter has laid out the basic recipe many LLMs use.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The value of LLMs does not depend on them being human-level learners: being able to talk to software in plain language is already a large practical shift. The 'basic recipe' refers to everything built in the chapter: a decoder-only Transformer pretrained on next-token prediction (mini-GPT, p.494–508), then instruction fine-tuning, LoRA, RLHF and the other extensions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames the chapter's code as the real blueprint behind production LLMs, differing mainly in scale (as the authors noted on p.508).

terminology.meaning: A way to control or query software by writing ordinary language instead of using code or menus.

connections: p.508: 'The training recipe we used previously is the exact blueprint used by everyone training LLMs today.'

paragraphs.excerpt: Large language models, or LLMs, are the combination of a few key ingredients
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: LLMs combine the Transformer architecture, a language-modeling task (predicting the next token from past tokens) and a large amount of unlabeled text data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These are exactly the ingredients GPT-1 combined in 2018 (p.493). None is new on its own; the power comes from the combination at scale. Because next-token prediction derives its targets from the text itself, the data needs no human labels — that is why 'unlabeled' text can be used in such quantity.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: If you can explain why each of the three ingredients is necessary, you understand the core of every modern LLM.

terminology.meaning: Learning $P(x_t \mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})$, the probability of the next token given the previous ones.
Training where the targets come from the input data itself (here, the next token), so no manual labels are needed.

connections: p.493: GPT combined unsupervised language-model pretraining, the Transformer and textual data from thousands of books.
p.494–502: the mini-GPT built and pretrained in this chapter uses this exact recipe.

paragraphs.excerpt: An LLM learns a probability distribution for predicting individual tokens. This can be combined
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: the LLM outputs a probability distribution over the next token; combined with a sampling strategy it generates long text. Greedy search picks the most likely token each step; random sampling samples directly from the full categorical distribution; top-K sampling restricts that distribution to the K most likely candidates.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The model itself only scores one step. Generation is a loop — pick a token, append it, run the model again — and the picking rule matters a lot. Greedy decoding is deterministic and tends to get stuck in repetitive loops; pure random sampling is diverse but can wander into nonsense, especially at high temperature; top-K is a middle ground that removes the long tail of unlikely tokens before sampling.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The same trained weights can produce dull, wild or reasonable text depending only on the sampling strategy, so it is a key control at inference time.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Temperature (p.506) rescales the logits before softmax and can be combined with either random or top-K sampling.

terminology.meaning: Choose $\arg\max$ of the predicted distribution at each step.
Draw the next token from the full softmax distribution (optionally temperature-scaled).
Keep only the K highest-probability tokens, renormalize, and sample among them.

connections: p.504–505: greedy search and its tendency to repeat.
p.506: random sampling and the temperature parameter.
p.508: beam search is mentioned as another strategy.

paragraphs.excerpt: LLMs use billions of parameters and are trained on trillions of words of text.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary bullet: LLMs have billions of parameters and are trained on trillions of words.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Scale is the remaining ingredient: the recipe above only produces today's capabilities at these sizes. The mini-GPT in this chapter is far smaller; p.508 estimates it would need at least 100× more parameters and 1,000× more training steps to reach modern quality.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It connects to the cost, energy and memory issues raised throughout the chapter (p.508, p.514) and to the data scarcity discussed on this page.

terminology.meaning: Training data size is usually measured in tokens (subword units); the summary's 'words' is an approximation.

connections: p.508: environmental and financial cost of pretraining (Llama 2 needed ~1.3 million kWh).
p.529: figure 16.8 plots these parameter and data scales over time.

concepts.name: Compute-optimal scaling (model size vs. data)
concepts.definition: For a fixed training compute budget, there is a best split between model parameters and training tokens; GPT-3 put too much into parameters.
concepts.intuition: A big brain that has read too little underperforms a smaller brain that has read much more, for the same total effort.
concepts.technical: Training flops grow roughly with parameters × tokens. Empirical studies (beyond the book: Hoffmann et al., 2022, 'Chinchilla') found compute-optimal models use roughly 20 tokens per parameter, far more than GPT-3's ~1.7.
concepts.significance: Explains the trend on p.529–530: data sizes grew steadily while parameter counts flattened or varied.
concepts.example: Training a smaller model on more tokens can beat a 175B-parameter model with the same compute.
concepts.misconception: That progress requires ever-larger parameter counts.

concepts.name: Deployment cost trade-off
concepts.definition: Choosing a smaller model than the best-performing one so it runs on cheaper hardware.
concepts.intuition: A model you cannot afford to serve to users is of little practical use.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: inference memory and latency scale with parameter count; a smaller model trained on more tokens can be cheaper to serve at similar quality.
concepts.significance: One of the two reasons the book gives for varied parameter counts after GPT-3.
concepts.example: The book uses a 1-billion-parameter Gemma 3 model because it fits on a free Colab GPU (p.509).
concepts.misconception: That the largest available model is always the right choice.

concepts.name: Pretraining data scarcity
concepts.definition: The supply of high-quality, public, human-written text is limited, constraining further scaling of dataset size.
concepts.intuition: You can buy more GPUs, but not more books that humans have already written.
concepts.technical: Training on LLM-generated text ('eating their own tail') risks reinforcing errors and losing diversity.
concepts.significance: Motivates alternative training signals such as reinforcement learning.
concepts.example: A web crawl increasingly contains AI-written pages, which then end up in the next model's training set.
concepts.misconception: That data is unlimited because the internet keeps growing — much new content is low quality or machine-generated.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning from a self-contained environment
concepts.definition: Training a model by letting it attempt problems produced by an environment and learning from feedback on its own outputs.
concepts.intuition: Like a student doing endless practice problems with an answer key, instead of reading more textbooks.
concepts.technical: For LLMs the environment can generate verifiable tasks (math, code); correct trajectories are rewarded or kept for fine-tuning (p.527–528).
concepts.significance: Supplies fresh training signal without new human-written text.
concepts.example: Sampling several chain-of-thought solutions to a math problem, checking the final answers, and fine-tuning on the correct ones.
concepts.misconception: That RL for LLMs always needs human raters — RLHF does, but verifiable environments do not.

concepts.name: Sampling strategy
concepts.definition: The rule that turns the model's next-token distribution into an actual token during generation.
concepts.intuition: The model proposes odds; the sampling strategy decides how adventurous to be when betting.
concepts.technical: Greedy: argmax. Random: sample the softmax (possibly temperature-scaled). Top-K: zero out all but the K largest probabilities, renormalize, sample.
concepts.significance: Strongly affects the quality and diversity of generated text with the same model.
concepts.example: Greedy decoding of the mini-GPT got stuck repeating phrases; top-K produced more plausible English (p.505–508).
concepts.misconception: That generation quality is determined entirely by the trained model.

concepts.name: Large language model (LLM)
concepts.definition: A Transformer trained to predict the next token on a large amount of unlabeled text, with billions of parameters.
concepts.technical: Learns $P(x_t\mid x_{<t})$ with cross-entropy loss; generation repeatedly samples from this distribution.
concepts.misconception: That LLMs store facts reliably — they model likely text, which is why they hallucinate (p.531).

math.title: The three sampling strategies in the summary (formalized)
math.latex: \begin{aligned} p_i &= \frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}} \\ \text{greedy: } x_t &= \arg\max_i p_i \\ \text{random: } x_t &\sim \operatorname{Categorical}(p) \\ \text{top-}K\text{: } x_t &\sim \operatorname{Categorical}(\tilde p),\quad \tilde p_i = \frac{p_i\,\mathbb{1}[i\in \mathcal{K}]}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}} p_j} \end{aligned}
math.source_text: Greedy search takes the most likely predicted token at each generation step. Random sampling directly samples the predicted categorical distribution over all tokens. Top-K sampling restricts the categorical distribution to the top set of K candidates.

variables.meaning: logit for vocabulary token i output by the model at the current step
temperature (T = 1 is the plain softmax; p.506)
the set of the K tokens with the largest probabilities
the renormalized distribution restricted to the top K
the token chosen at step t

math.operations: Softmax over logits, then argmax, unrestricted sampling, or truncate-and-renormalize sampling.
math.purpose: Make precise the verbal definitions in the summary bullet.
math.interpretation: Greedy is the limit of random sampling as T → 0; top-K with K = 1 also equals greedy, and with K = vocabulary size equals random sampling.
math.intuition: Top-K cuts off the long tail of implausible tokens that pure random sampling occasionally picks.
math.numerical_example: Probabilities over 4 tokens: [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]. Greedy always picks token 1. Random sampling picks token 4 5% of the time. Top-2 renormalizes to [0.625, 0.375, 0, 0], so tokens 3 and 4 can never be picked.

deeper.title: Why train smaller than 'compute-optimal'?
deeper.body:
Beyond the book. Use the common approximation that training costs about $6ND$ flops and generating one token costs about $2N$ flops.

- Model A: $N = 70$B, $D = 1.4$T tokens → training ≈ $5.9\times10^{23}$ flops; each generated token ≈ $1.4\times10^{11}$ flops.
- Model B: $N = 8$B, $D = 15$T tokens → training ≈ $7.2\times10^{23}$ flops (similar); each generated token ≈ $1.6\times10^{10}$ flops, almost 9× cheaper.

If the model will serve billions of requests, B's per-query savings dwarf its slightly higher training cost. This is the 'practical reason' the authors give for varied parameter counts.

deeper.title: Imitation vs. practice
deeper.body: Pretraining is like learning a language by reading every book in a library; once you have read them all, more reading isn't available. RL in a self-contained environment is like a chess player who keeps improving by playing games and seeing who won: the games are generated on demand and the outcome provides the feedback. The book's point is that this kind of signal does not run out the way human-written text does.

deeper.title: How the chapter's pieces map onto the summary
deeper.body:
- **Transformer** → the decoder blocks of mini-GPT (16.2.1, p.497).
- **Language-modeling task** → next-token pretraining (16.2.2, p.500).
- **Unlabeled text** → the pretraining corpus used for mini-GPT and, at far larger scale, for Gemma.
- **Sampling strategy** → 16.2.3–16.2.4 (p.502–508).
- **Scale** → section 16.5 and figure 16.8 (p.528–529).

The continuation on p.531 covers instruction fine-tuning, memory/LoRA, multimodality and foundation models.

visualizations.title: From logits to a sampling distribution
visualizations.why: The summary says an LLM learns a probability distribution for the next token and that greedy, random and top-K sampling use it differently. Move the logits and temperature to see how peaked the distribution is — the argmax is what greedy picks, and the tail is what top-K removes.

misconceptions.claim: LLM progress simply means more parameters every year.
misconceptions.correction: Figure 16.8 and this page show parameter counts varying since GPT-3 while data sizes climb; compute-optimal training and deployment cost both favor smaller models trained on more data.

misconceptions.claim: Training on text generated by other LLMs is a free way to get more data.
misconceptions.correction: The authors call this 'eating their own tail' and note it brings its own host of concerns, such as propagating errors and losing diversity.

misconceptions.claim: Reinforcement learning for LLMs only means RLHF with human raters.
misconceptions.correction: This page describes self-contained environments that generate new problems, letting the model train on its own outputs with automatic feedback (as with the reasoning loop on p.527–528).

misconceptions.claim: Greedy search gives the best text because it always picks the most likely token.
misconceptions.correction: Greedy decoding tends to loop and repeat (p.505); top-K or temperature sampling usually gives more natural text.

takeaways: Since GPT-3, data sizes have grown steadily but parameter counts vary: GPT-3 was undertrained, and smaller models are cheaper to deploy.
High-quality human-written text is running out; training on LLM output raises new problems.
RL in self-contained environments lets models keep training on their own (checked) outputs.
LLMs are far less sample-efficient than humans; research on learning from limited data will continue.
LLM = Transformer + next-token prediction + lots of unlabeled text, at the scale of billions of parameters and trillions of words.
Greedy, random and top-K sampling turn the same next-token distribution into very different text.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the authors offer for why parameter counts have varied since GPT-3 even as training data grew.
questions.answer: GPT-3 is now known to have been undertrained (too many parameters for its data/compute), and in deployment a smaller model that runs on cheaper hardware is often worth a small loss in performance.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the first paragraph; the undertraining point refers back to the compute-budget argument on p.528.

questions.question: According to the page, why is reinforcement learning attracting attention as a way to continue training LLMs?
options: It removes the need for a Transformer architecture
A self-contained environment can generate new problems so the model trains on its own output instead of more web text
It makes models smaller and cheaper to deploy
It guarantees that models no longer hallucinate
questions.answer: A self-contained environment can generate new problems so the model trains on its own output instead of more web text
questions.explanation: The authors link RL directly to running out of pretraining data. RL does not replace the Transformer, is not presented as a model-compression method, and the summary on p.531 explicitly says all LLMs still hallucinate.

questions.question: Why might training on large amounts of LLM-generated text be a concern, in light of the authors' 'eat their own tail' remark?
questions.answer: The new model learns to imitate another model's output distribution, including its errors and blind spots, rather than human-written text; repeated over generations this can amplify mistakes and reduce diversity.
questions.explanation: The book only says it 'runs into a whole other host of concerns'; the specific mechanisms (error propagation, loss of diversity) are an AI explanation of why that feedback loop is problematic.

questions.question: Which sampling strategy restricts the categorical distribution to a fixed number of the most likely candidates before sampling?
questions.explanation: Top-K keeps only the K most likely tokens. Greedy always takes the single most likely token without sampling; random sampling uses the whole distribution; beam search (p.508) keeps several candidate sequences rather than truncating a single-step distribution for sampling.

questions.question: A model predicts probabilities [0.6, 0.25, 0.1, 0.05] for four tokens. What is the probability of picking the second token under (a) greedy search, (b) random sampling, (c) top-2 sampling?
questions.explanation: Greedy deterministically picks the argmax (token 1). Random sampling uses the probabilities as given. Top-2 keeps tokens 1 and 2 and renormalizes by their sum 0.85.

questions.question: What are the three key ingredients of an LLM according to the chapter summary?
questions.answer: The Transformer architecture, a language-modeling task (predicting the next token from past tokens), and a large amount of unlabeled text data.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first summary bullet; they match the ingredients of the original GPT (p.493).

questions.question: Can you explain, in your own words, what the authors mean by 'LLMs are wildly inefficient at learning compared to humans,' and why that suggests scaling alone isn't the full answer?
questions.answer: LLMs need orders of magnitude more text than a human ever reads to reach their abilities; if data is running out and humans learn from far less, better learning algorithms (not only more data and compute) are needed.
questions.explanation: Check that your answer links the inefficiency point to the data-scarcity paragraph and mentions research into learning quickly from limited data.
